newsitem.title: USA: MSRB issues "election year reminder" to dealers.
newsitem.headline: MSRB issues "election year reminder" to dealers.

text.p: The MSRB said on Tuesday it will issue an "election year reminder" to municipal bond dealers and their political action committees this week that their political contributions can trigger an underwriting ban under the board's pay-to-play rule.
Enacted in April 1994, rule G-37 bars municipal bond dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments.
According to an advance copy of MSRB Reports, the board's quarterly report to dealers, the panel is reminding dealers that rule G-37 covers more than just direct contributions to issuer candidates.
The rule also covers money given to a candidate for transition or inaugural expenses and to pay off election debts, the MSRB notice says.

"The board wishes to remind dealers that any contributions given by a dealer or dealer-controlled PAC for the above purposes for the benefit of an issuer official would lead to a two-year ban on municipal securities business with the issuer," the notice says.
The rule's de minimis exception let's muni professionals contribution up to $250 per election if a professional is entitled to vote for that official.
MSRB reminds dealers that the de minimis exemption is keyed to an election cycle.

That means if a muni professional gives $250 to a candidate's general election, the professional could not make contributions for transition or inaugural expenses without triggering a ban on business, MSRB says.

The notice adds if a muni professional made no contributions to an issuer official before the election, then the professional can, if entitled to vote for the candidate, give up to $250 for transition or inaugural expenses and election debt payments without triggering the ban.
MSRB's notice adds if a candidate loses an election, that candidate is no longer considered an issuer official.
So any money given to a candidate to help pay off election debts, would not be covered by rule G-37, MSRB says.
